title: 10 Cases of Mistaken Identity
summary: Josh and Chuck count down a "top ten" list of cases of mistaken identity, opening with a tour reminder. Cases covered: an Australian ex-pat (Nicole McCabe) whose real identity was used as cover by Israel's Mossad during the Dubai killing of Hamas figure Mahmoud al-Mabhouh; the 1903-era William West case, where a man with the same name and Bertillon measurements was wrongly booked into Leavenworth until fingerprints cleared it; Adolph Beck, wrongly convicted of fraud crimes committed by "John Smith"/Lord Willoughby, and the resulting Court of Appeal; medical identity theft against Anne Dorree Sacks, whose ID was stolen and used to give birth and rack up a $10,000 bill; Peter Hampikian, a British bartender matched by a DNA profile in an Italian murder case, and the limits of DNA matching; a bone marrow transplant that made an Alaskan man's DNA match his brother's, leading to a sexual assault mix-up; identical twins in Germany (Kaufhof department store robbery) whom DNA could not distinguish; the 2006 Michigan crash in which Whitney Sarachman was misidentified as Laura Van Wrin; and Peter Sellers being mistaken for Woody Allen on the set of Casino Royale (1967) and What's New Pussycat. The episode closes with listener mail about Chuck's 'rope trauma' and a sign-off.

segments.title: Tour reminder and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh gives a tour reminder for February Pacific Northwest dates, then introduces the episode as a top ten list of mistaken identity cases.

segments.title: Israeli agents use real identities; Nicole McCabe in Dubai
segments.summary: Nicole McCabe, a pregnant Australian ex-pat in Israel, saw her passport shown on TV as one of twenty-six people sought over the Dubai killing of Hamas figure Mahmoud al-Mabhouh. The hosts explain Mossad used real foreigners' identities as cover, and Australia offered her a new passport.

segments.title: William West and Leavenworth Bertillon mix-up
segments.summary: William West was booked at Leavenworth on manslaughter charges, but his Bertillon measurements matched another prisoner with the same name, who was already serving a life sentence. Fingerprints cleared him and replaced the Bertillon method.

segments.title: Adolph Beck wrongly convicted of fraud
segments.summary: Adolph Beck was convicted of jewelry fraud committed by a con man using names such as John Smith and Lord Willoughby, serving seven years despite evidence he was abroad. He was later convicted again and then released after press pressure, receiving compensation, and the case contributed to the creation of the Court of Appeal.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before the next case.

segments.title: Medical identity theft: Anne Dorree Sacks
segments.summary: Anne Dorree Sacks's identity was used by a drug-addicted woman who had stolen her ID from a car, gave birth, and left a $10,000 medical bill. Sacks was disbelieved until a DNA test proved she was not the mother. The hosts discuss privacy laws that blocked her from seeing her altered records.

segments.title: Peter Hampikian and DNA match limits
segments.summary: British bartender Peter Hampikian was arrested after a DNA match in a 2002 Italian murder case, despite never having been to Italy. Later, a further DNA profile using more markers cleared him. The hosts explain loci, how many markers are used, and the risk of false matches.

segments.title: Bone marrow transplant DNA and Alaska brothers
segments.summary: An Alaskan sexual assault case matched a jailed man's DNA, but he had received a bone marrow transplant from his brother, so his blood carried the brother's DNA. The hosts also mention Chris Long, whose tissues carried donor DNA after a German transplant.

segments.title: Identical twins and the Kaufhof robbery
segments.summary: In Germany, DNA from sweat in a glove left at a 2009 department store robbery matched two identical twins, who each denied involvement. Authorities could not charge either without risking an innocent person. The hosts note similar twin cases in Malaysia.

segments.title: 2006 Michigan van crash misidentification
segments.summary: After a 2006 crash involving a Taylor University van, first responders put the wrong ID on Whitney Sarachman, who was alive, while Laura Van Wrin, who had died, was recorded as the survivor. Families were confused until Sarachman wrote her name.

segments.title: Peter Sellers mistaken for Woody Allen
segments.summary: Peter Sellers was repeatedly mistaken for Woody Allen on set, including Casino Royale (1967) where studio head Leo Jaffe complained to him as if he were Allen, and on What's New Pussycat.

segments.title: Listener mail: Chuck's rope trauma
segments.summary: Listener Ryan asks about Chuck's rope trauma, which Chuck declines to explain. The hosts invite guesses by email.
